title: The Jesuits suppressed (1773)
hook: the pope dissolves the Jesuits under political pressure; they are restored in 1814

segments.voice: Yesterday, Junípero Serra, honestly: a saint to some, a wound to others. Your line was listen first. Today, an order of missionaries is itself sent away.

What happens to an order when the pope himself shuts it down? In a cell in the Castel Sant'Angelo, the old fortress by the Tiber in Rome, sits an elderly priest, Lorenzo Ricci, superior general of the Society of Jesus, the Jesuits, the order Ignatius founded. Except the order he leads no longer exists. The pope has dissolved it. Its houses are closed, its schools taken from it, its priests scattered. Ricci is questioned, kept in custody, and never released. He dies a prisoner. Today, how an order of teachers and missionaries came to this.
screen: `A CELL BY THE TIBER.` → `THE JESUIT GENERAL, A PRISONER.` → `HIS ORDER IS GONE.`

segments.voice: First, the kings. The decisive pressure didn't come from outside the Church. It came from Catholic courts. Portugal, France and Spain had already thrown the Jesuits out of their lands and seized their property, for tangled reasons: politics, money, quarrels over missions and schools, resentment of the order's influence. Then those courts pressed the pope to finish the job everywhere. Second, the pen. Pope Clement the Fourteenth gave way. He signed a brief, known by its opening Latin words, Dominus ac Redemptor, the Lord and Redeemer, dissolving the Society for the sake of the peace of the Church. It gave no verdict of heresy. In country after country, Jesuits laid down their order's name. They obeyed. Third, the thread that didn't break. In the Russian Empire, Catherine the Great refused to publish the brief, so it never took effect there, and a small group of Jesuits quietly carried on. Fourth, restored. Decades later, Pope Pius the Seventh restored the Society of Jesus for the whole Church. The same Church that dissolved them brought them back, and the thread from Russia was part of what was rewoven. Saint Paul knew seasons like this. In Second Corinthians, in the Douay-Rheims: "we suffer persecution, but are not forsaken; we are cast down, but we perish not." Unfair seasons are real. So, in this story, are restorations.
screen: `CATHOLIC KINGS PRESS THE POPE.` · `A BRIEF DISSOLVES THE ORDER.` · `A THREAD SURVIVES IN RUSSIA.` · `RESTORED BY PIUS VII.` · then, large: `CAST DOWN, BUT WE PERISH NOT.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something unfair you're living with, at work, at home, in your body, in a decision someone else made, and name it plainly, without exaggerating or shrinking it. Then ask what the Jesuits in Russia had to ask: what one small thing can I keep doing faithfully, right here? If you pray, place the whole season in God's hands; if not, let yourself hold it without hurrying it.
Lorenzo Ricci. The last superior general before the pope dissolved the Jesuits, kept in custody at the Castel Sant'Angelo, who died a prisoner.
Your line: restored. The story didn't end where the brief was signed. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Jesuits today remember the suppression and restoration as part of their own story, and their schools, parishes and retreat houses often tell it to students and retreatants as a lesson in obedience and endurance.

chat.says: Did a pope really shut down the Jesuits once? Why?
options: Yes. Catholic kings pressed him into it; decades later, another pope restored them.
Yes. A Church court found the Jesuits guilty of heresy, so they were dissolved.
No. Only Spain expelled them; the pope never dissolved the whole order.
chat.meaning: Pressure from Catholic courts led Clement XIV to dissolve the Society, with no verdict of heresy; Pius VII later restored it.

notes: Claims rule: the dates 1773 and 1814 stay in the index title and hook but are not spoken; 'decades later' is used for the restoration. Confirm 'decades later' is acceptable.
Lorenzo Ricci held in Castel Sant'Angelo, never convicted, died in custody: confirm phrasing ('questioned, kept in custody, and never released').
'A few weeks back on this path' refers to the Society's founding (day 849); confirm the distance reads right.
Order of expulsions (Portugal, France, Spain) and their reasons summarized; confirm.
'It gave no verdict of heresy': the brief lists complaints and cites the peace of the Church; confirm.
Survival in the Russian Empire under Catherine II and its role in the restoration: confirm 'part of what was rewoven'.
'Catholic courts' pressure: Naples and Parma also pressed; only the three main courts named.

Editor: hook now opens with a question instead of another 'A [place]...' fragment, and the closing 'pope's own army' line is replaced; 'Jesuits around the world' (which contradicted the Russian survival) changed to 'in country after country'.
Editor 2: fixed the hook clause that made the order sound founded 'a few weeks back'; cut the unsupported 'in a place nobody would have chosen'.

Auditor: 'schools emptied' changed to 'taken from it' (many colleges were handed to others, not emptied); the claim that pressure 'didn't come from the Jesuits' enemies outside the Church' softened to 'the decisive pressure', since Jansenist and Enlightenment critics also fed the campaign. Prussia (Frederick II) also declined to promulgate the brief; only Russia is named.
